title: Ask HN: Who's really winning with AI-Coding?
text:
I've noticed the same pattern across three different Claude-coded projects now. Initial velocity is strong, but starts to fade until returns are negative.

It seems a combination of changes in model behavior and increasing code base size—emphasis on the latter. The larger the code base and documented history/progress (e.g. through updates to completed work and instructions, as in .md files), the more drift starts to set in.

At a certain point, you get collapse. This is where it can't maintain consistency within a single unit of work. It can manifest, for example, as adding a similar element to a view, but styling it in a completely different manner than existing elements. It literally feels random.

It can also manifest as incoherent or poorly implemented logic and behavior. I've followed different advice, restructured projects, entered plan mode, added deterministic checks, styles, rules, etc. But, it feels like whack-a-mole and it's unclear that it actually adheres to these rules in the first place.

Then, there's the question of it moving the problem. In response to my complaints of inconsistent UI generation, it recommended a style check to run after its UI changes. Of course, that begs the question of why it doesn't just apply those rules in the initial generation.

But, I am at a place now where it spins up AI agents to do a full UI/UX review—Playwright and all. Yet, it's still drifting and not catching it. This is consistent with its unit tests—on my latest project it has now generated a suite of hundreds of somewhat time consuming tests that it constantly runs pre-commit, and not a single test has ever failed. Meanwhile, there have been a number of bugs. When questioned, it said it had been testing the "wrong layer" and had essentially generated self-confirming tests.

My question is who is really winning here? When querying Google, it points to so many claims of success and approaches that supposedly contribute to that success. But, when you break down the underlying source for those claims, it appears to be largely Reddit.

Yet, pressing it further reveals that virtually every actual study shows either little to no productivity gains or actual regression—particularly where experienced engineers are concerned. And some of those studies debunk the self-reported claims of exactly the kind you see on Reddit, etc.

So, who here has developed a quality production application of any complexity using AI coding? If anyone, which harness/model, and what techniques did you use? Also, can you point us to your repo?
author: unclebucknasty

title: Re: Show HN: Standard Support – a convention for AI ag...
text:
Hi HN, I'm Nathan, the founder of DocSpring [1] (an API for filling in and signing documents).

We recently put a lot of work into our MCP server and API, because more of our customers' setup work is done by their AI agents: creating templates, testing them with tool calls, and writing their integrations. We get error reports automatically, but a lot of bugs and friction never reach us unless someone tells us about it.

I asked one of my AI agents to help me write up how an agent could report a problem and get an answer back. We decided on four MCP tools (open a ticket, list, read, reply), the same operations over HTTP, and a status URL per ticket that a background script can poll. Some people set up email inboxes for their agents, but most people running Claude Code probably won't have those set up. We also decided that tickets belong to the customer, not the ephemeral agent session, so a fresh session tomorrow can pick up any replies.

A few projects already do something like this. What I couldn't find was a written-down set of decisions anyone could copy. You can consider this more of a suggestion and a reference implementation than a "standard", but I liked the name Standard Support. Nothing breaks if you implement it differently, and you're free to build your own support tools that work differently. Agents will read the tool descriptions either way.

We haven't shipped it in DocSpring yet and it's still a WIP draft. I decided to publish this early because I'd be interested in hearing your feedback. For example, what do you think about the following:

- Polling a status URL instead of webhooks. Coding agents could make this easier by letting an agent keep an MCP tool call polling in the background. There's also work on MCP Tasks and MCP Events [2].

- The default that the agent asks the user before opening a ticket. I actually lean towards inviting more reports for our own product, but I didn't want the default to flood anyone's inbox. However, we worked with a partner recently and their AI agent gave us a huge list of feedback for how we can improve our API to work better with HTML templates. There were a lot of really good suggestions and we implemented almost everything.

- The rules for when agents are on both sides of a ticket. Reports and replies are both untrusted text. This is the thing that worries me the most. We don't do automated support at DocSpring (although we use AI tools to help us with tickets.) I believe that some companies go all-in on agentic support workflows where a support agent can even push fixes to production.

We've included a reference server and an agent skill in the repo [3] in case you would like to explore this further.

[1] https://docspring.com

[2] https://modelcontextprotocol.io/community/working-groups/tas...

[3] https://github.com/DocSpring/standardsupport

title: Show HN: Goethe – turn your computer into an inference engine
text:
Hi HN, I'm Matteo from meshapplied (YC W27), building this with Peter and Janos.

We think you can and should own your inference, so we built software that actually supports that. Goethe turns a Linux machine with an NVIDIA GPU into an API your OpenAI, Anthropic compatible clients can call.

``` curl -fsSL https://goethe.sh/install.sh | bash goethe start ```

Limits: it's Linux only rn and it supports Ampere or newer NVIDIA GPUs. Logging in with `goethe login` is optional and turns on the optimized kernels.

Docs: [goethe.sh/docs](https://goethe.sh/docs)

I'd love to hear what breaks and what you'd want next.

title: Show HN: My OSS Claude Meetings alternative that works with any agent or call
text:
Since February, I've been developing an agent-in-calls solution with a friend. With the announcement of Claude Meetings last week, it's now time to announce Vibeconferencing: an open-source project with even more functionality, support for any agent (Codex, Muse, local ollama, etc), and support for more calling platforms: Google Meet, Zoom, MS Teams, WhatsApp, Telegram, and phone calls (via Twilio).

Architecture diagram: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wanderingstan/vibeconf-app...

The premise is simple: give your normal agent session the tools it needs to operate all major calling platforms, and teach it basic etiquette of how to behave in a call with others. A simple `/join-call` and boom! your session is talking to you in the call. Anything your agent can do in chat, it can do on the call. The agent is bridged to the calling platforms via a cross-platform electron app. (The raw guts of interacting with calling platforms is abstracted as the npm library `@vibeconferencing/calls`, if you'd rather roll your own.)

Everything runs locally and uses your own local agent. (Tho the optional shared whiteboard feature does require being logged in on our server.) It runs on MacOS, Windows, and Linux. (Windows version is not well tested.)

Speech generation is done either by Elevenlabs or the OSS Voicebox, with a fallback to the OS's default app (e.g. `say` on MacOS). Voicebox: https://github.com/jamiepine/voicebox

Speech recognition is done either by the calling platforms' own captioning services (Meet, Zoom, Teams), or with Whistle for those without captioning (WhatsApp, Telegram, Twilio). Whistle: https://cactuscompute.com/blog/whistle

The etiquette was the most fun to code, although done with the knowledge that it's a temporary fix until true interactive voice models are merged with the power of frontier text chat models. We have experimental support for the OpenAI realtime API, but it seems to have been trained as a customer support agent, so it's hard to keep it from dominating multi-person conversations!

Highlights from the last nine months of dogfooding and early users:

- A WhatsApp bot for my father, an elderly WW2 veteran, that has access to the 20,000 photos he scanned. He can call it to see and hear about any aspect of his life. https://youtu.be/Rs-Z1YeLt98

- Collaboratively built a website for a friend's non-profit, with her amazed that she could ask for site changes and see the site change in realtime. https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iSRgY8JGJ0liOzHMl2bOGNd9jwq...

- My friend Matt is currently road-tripping across the US, talking with his Codex sessions to develop his Golf app. https://youtu.be/a3uNUdIwqVY

- Our friend Bethany uses her bot "Taylor Script", in calls and classrooms with coding students to act as the super-smart TA who can answer technical questions, and monitors student progress. https://youtu.be/c8mZKkcxhJo

- I begin most days with a check-in call with my bot Jimmy, where we discuss open repo issues while I have breakfast. https://youtu.be/2uQIR83LwY0 (Apologies for eating with my mouth open...)

- In a standup, Seth's bot created a video ad for the service itself, within a call. https://x.com/vibeconf/status/2104427917816234257?s=20

Security: There is nothing built in, so only use this on calls with people that you trust. However, I've been amazed at how injection-resistant it has appeared to be on it's own; e.g. my agent asking consent from me before doing things asked by others on the call.

Overall, this was a "time machine" experiment (to borrow my old Reality Labs' Research terminology) to experience agents-in-calls before it was purpose built. Claude Meetings just showed that we were thinking in the right direction, and I'm excited to see where this goes!

This is a small experimental project built by two friends, so it is rough around the edges, and we'd love feedback and pull requests.

title: Re: How to Intercept HTTP/3 Traffic: QUIC and Qpack...
text:
The key requirement here is the client has to trust the proxy's CA. It's a client-side MITM, and the article itself notes pinned apps reject it. QUIC's crypto is fine. HTTP/3 just stopped being a blind spot for corporate TLS-inspection boxes.

It's more interesting to split tunnel designs by where the trust lives:

- ngrok / Cloudflare Tunnel: the edge terminates TLS by design, and your public hostname is ordinary WebPKI. Anyone who controls a visitor's trust store (inspection appliance, malware root cert) can do exactly this, and the provider can see plaintext anyway.

- iroh-style P2P QUIC: there's no CA in the loop. You dial a public key (the EndpointId), and the TLS handshake authenticates raw keys, so it's pinned by construction. Relays forward ciphertext they can't terminate. A rogue root cert gets an attacker nothing; they'd need the peer's secret key.

So "can someone MITM my HTTP/3?" really comes down to "who can add to the set of keys my client trusts?" For WebPKI that's a long list. For key-addressed transports it's nobody: the trusted key is the address you dialed, unless an endpoint's secret key (or the machine itself) is already compromised.

title: Show HN: View – Build native Mac Mini apps with your own coding agent
text:
View runs small rust programs as native interfaces using Rust and GPUI. Coding agents write and edit the programs. Changes load without restarting the app.

Each view has its own state and permissions. Views access data through APIs, CLIs or MCP servers.

It supports Pi, Codex, Claude Code and OpenCode and more. Saved state is encrypted locally. Credentials are stored in macOS Keychain.
